title: Merge Sort
tagline: Split, sort the halves, then merge — stable O(n log n) sorting and the engine behind inversion counting.

intuition.analogy: Imagine sorting a huge stack of exam papers with a friend. You split the stack in half, each of you sorts your half (recursively splitting again), then you merge the two sorted piles by repeatedly taking the smaller top sheet. Merging two already-sorted piles is easy and linear.
paragraphs: Merge sort is the cleanest example of divide and conquer. Sorting a big array is hard, but sorting two halves and combining them is manageable — and combining two sorted arrays is a simple linear scan with two pointers.

The recursion tree has depth log n (you can only halve n down to 1 about log n times), and each level does O(n) total work to merge everything back. log n levels × O(n) per level = O(n log n), regardless of the input order. No worst case to fear.
Merge sort is stable (equal elements keep their relative order) and its access pattern is sequential, which is why variants of it power external sorting and standard library 'stable_sort'.
intuition.keyIdea: Merging two sorted halves is linear, so recursively sorting halves gives O(n log n) overall.

steps.title: Divide
steps.detail: Split the range [l, r] at the midpoint m. Recurse on [l, m] and [m+1, r] until ranges have one element (already sorted).

steps.title: Merge
steps.detail: Use two pointers over the two sorted halves, always copying the smaller front element into the output. Ties take the left element first to preserve stability.

steps.title: Copy back
steps.detail: Write the merged result back into the original positions. A single shared buffer of size n avoids repeated allocations.

complexity.timeReason: log n levels of recursion, each performing O(n) merge work across all segments.
complexity.spaceReason: A temporary buffer holds merged output; recursion adds O(log n) stack.

pitfalls: Allocating a new buffer inside every merge call destroys performance — share one buffer.
Using '<' instead of '<=' when merging breaks stability.
Computing midpoint as (l+r)/2 risks overflow on very large indices.

rows: Merge two sorted halves with two pointers
dryRun.clickMoment: The work happens on the way back up. Singletons are trivially sorted; every merge step combines two already-sorted runs, so you never compare more than necessary.

approach: Textbook merge sort: split in half, sort each half recursively, then merge the two sorted halves in linear time.
It is stable and guaranteed O(n log n) regardless of input, at the cost of O(n) auxiliary space for merging.

problems.title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self
problems.statement: For each element, count how many elements to its right are smaller.
problems.hint: During merge, when you take an element from the right half, every remaining left element is greater — count those crossings.
problems.tests: Counting inversions inside the merge step.

approach: While merging, every time an element from the right half is placed before remaining left-half elements, those left elements are all greater and were originally to its left — a counting opportunity.
Sort indices (not values) so we can record counts per original position. When we take a left element, add the number of right elements already merged.

problems.title: Reverse Pairs
problems.statement: Count pairs (i, j) with i < j and a[i] > 2·a[j].
problems.hint: Add a counting pass before merging each level, using the two sorted halves.
problems.tests: Modified merge for a custom inversion condition.

approach: A reverse pair is i < j with a[i] > 2*a[j]. Count them during merge sort: before merging two sorted halves, for each left element count right elements it dominates.
Because both halves are sorted, the count pointer only moves forward, so the extra counting pass is linear per merge.

problems.title: Merge k Sorted Lists
problems.statement: Merge k sorted linked lists into one sorted list.
problems.hint: Divide and conquer: pair up lists and merge them, halving the count each round.
problems.tests: Generalising the merge step to k inputs.

approach: Merging k lists pairwise from the front is O(kn); instead apply divide and conquer — merge lists in pairs so the number of lists halves each round.
log k rounds, each touching all n nodes once, gives O(n log k). Each pairwise merge is the standard two-list merge.

problems.title: Sort List
problems.statement: Sort a linked list in O(n log n) and O(1) extra space (besides recursion).
problems.hint: Use fast/slow pointers to split the list, then merge — merge sort is ideal for linked lists.
problems.tests: Merge sort adapted to linked lists.

approach: Merge sort is the natural O(n log n) sort for a linked list: it needs no random access and only O(1) pointer rewiring to merge.
Find the middle with slow/fast pointers, cut the list in two, sort each half recursively, then merge the two sorted halves.
